title: A one-page CV
objectives: Write a one-page CV whose every line shows a skill an interviewer can test.

screens.title: Lines you could be asked about
screens.prose: Sam's draft CV is below. In an interview, any line on it can become a question. Some give an interviewer nothing to ask about. Scroll the table to the end.

rows: Sam Reid, London; email and phone
Hard-working team player with a passion for markets
Probability, Statistics, Numerical Methods, Stochastic Processes
Tested 12-month momentum on 20 years of UK shares; net Sharpe 0.4
Dice-game simulator in Python; checked 6 expected values against exact answers
Data intern, a small asset manager, Jun to Aug 2026
Cut a weekly report from 3 hours to 20 minutes with a Python script
Proficient in Python, C++, Java, R, MATLAB, SQL
Chess: club rating 1850; ran the society's league

state.caption: Sam is an invented candidate. One line per row, as the page reads top to bottom.

screens.question: Tap the four lines an interviewer could not test.

hints.text: For each line, ask: what question could follow, and could Sam answer it with a fact?
Adjectives and long lists are hard to test. So is a duty with no result.
The profile line, "Responsible for data analysis", the six-language list and "Reading, travel".

feedback.correct: Four lines with nothing to test.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only lines with no fact, number or result behind them.

byKey.r5: That line is testable: the interviewer can ask how the Sharpe ratio was worked out.
byKey.r9: That line has a result, 3 hours to 20 minutes. An interviewer can ask how.
byKey.r3: A predicted grade is a fact the university can confirm.
byKey.r12: A rating and a role are testable. Expect a question about the league.
byKey.r6: Six expected values checked against exact answers is a claim an interviewer can probe.
byKey.r11: A score is testable. Some trading interviews open with mental arithmetic.
byKey.r1: You missed the profile line. "Hard-working team player" gives nothing to check.
byKey.r8: You missed "Responsible for data analysis". It names a duty, not something Sam did.
byKey.r10: You missed the skills list. Six languages invite six questions Sam cannot all answer.
byKey.r13: You missed "Reading, travel". It is true of almost everyone, so it says nothing.

explain.text: The four weak lines state adjectives, a duty or a list. Every other line holds a fact, a number or a result that can be checked. **Every line is a claim an interviewer can test**, and some will.

screens.prose: You tapped lines with nothing behind them. A strong line is a **testable claim**: an interviewer asks "how?" and you answer with what you did.

rows: Cut a weekly report from 3 hours to 20 minutes with a Python script

screens.question: Which test does the highlighted line pass and the other fail?

options.text: Asked "how?", Sam can answer with a method and a number
It sounds more impressive
options.why: You judged by sound. Both lines could sound fine; only one can be checked.

options.text: It uses more of a posting's keywords
options.why: You judged by keywords. Keywords help a screen, but an interview checks the claim behind them.

options.text: It is shorter
options.why: You judged by length. The weak line is the shorter one here.

hints.text: Imagine the interviewer reading each line aloud and saying "tell me more".
One line names a duty; the other names a result.
The report line has a before, an after and a tool. The duty line has none.

feedback.correct: A method and a number behind it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which line Sam could defend for two minutes.

explain.text: "Responsible for data analysis" names a duty, so the follow-up has nowhere to go. "Cut a weekly report from 3 hours to 20 minutes" invites "how?", and Sam has an answer. That is the test for every line.

screens.prose: Now rewrite the weak duty line. At the asset manager, Sam cleaned price data and sped up a backtest.

rows: Data intern, a small asset manager, Jun to Aug 2026

screens.question: Which rewrite should replace "Responsible for data analysis"?

options.text: Cleaned 2 years of daily prices for 500 shares in pandas; cut a backtest from 40 to 6 minutes
Responsible for extensive, detailed and rigorous data analysis
options.why: You added adjectives. They add length, not anything an interviewer can check.

options.text: Analysed lots of data, improving efficiency significantly
options.why: You used vague amounts. "Lots" and "significantly" give the interviewer nothing to probe.

options.text: Built the firm's trading model, which made £2 million
options.why: You claimed a result Sam cannot defend. One question about what Sam built would expose it.

hints.text: Which rewrite says what Sam did, with what, and how much?
Look for a verb, a tool and a number.
"Cleaned ... in pandas; cut ... from 40 to 6 minutes" has all three, and Sam did it.

feedback.correct: A verb, a tool and two numbers, all Sam's own.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the line Sam could explain step by step.

explain.text: The rewrite starts with a verb, names the tool and gives two numbers. Every part is Sam's own work, so every follow-up has an answer. Going from 40 to 6 minutes is about 6.7 times faster; be ready to say how.

screens.prose: Sam's skills line lists six languages. Here is what Sam has actually done with each. List only what you could be tested in today.

columns: What Sam has done with it
rows: Two projects and the internship, most days
Queried the firm's price database every day of the internship
One online tutorial, two years ago
Opened it for one first-year lab

screens.question: Select all that apply: which languages belong on Sam's skills line?

options.text: Python
SQL
R

options.why: You kept C++ for one old tutorial. One C++ question in an interview would find that out.

options.text: Java
options.why: You kept Java for a single "Hello, world". That is not a skill an interviewer can test.

options.text: MATLAB
options.why: You kept MATLAB for one lab. Leave it off until you have used it.

hints.text: Which languages has Sam used for real work that someone checked?
Daily use, or marked coursework, counts.
Python, SQL and R. The other three were a tutorial, one line and one lab.

feedback.correct: Three languages, each one Sam could be tested in.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep a language only if Sam has used it for real work.

explain.text: Python, SQL and R each have work behind them that Sam can describe. A level helps: "Python (daily), SQL, R (coursework)". Three honest languages beat six thin ones.

screens.prose: Sam applies in London. UK conventions for a student CV are stricter than many people expect.

rows: "2024 to 2027" in one place, "Sept 24" in another

screens.question: Select all that apply: which changes does Sam's UK CV need?

options.text: Cut it to one page
Remove the photo
Remove the date of birth
Write every date in one format
Remove the predicted grade until it is achieved
options.why: You removed the grade. UK employers expect a predicted or achieved grade; leaving it out looks like hiding it.

options.text: Replace the grade with a GPA
options.why: You used the US scale. In the UK give the degree class or a percentage average.

hints.text: Which items could invite bias or waste space?
A photo and a date of birth say nothing about skill.
One page, no photo, no date of birth, one date format. Keep the predicted grade.

feedback.correct: One page, no photo, no date of birth, consistent dates.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the grade; remove what says nothing about skill.

explain.text: A UK undergraduate CV is one page, with no photo and no date of birth. Dates follow one format, and a predicted or achieved grade is expected. In the US the rules are the same, with a GPA in place of a degree class.

screens.prose: Sam has no finance job yet worth leading with. The order of sections tells a reader what to look at first.

rows: Tested 12-month momentum on 20 years of UK shares; net Sharpe 0.4
Data intern, a small asset manager, Jun to Aug 2026
Proficient in Python, C++, Java, R, MATLAB, SQL

screens.question: Put a student's CV sections in order, top to bottom. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.why: You kept a career objective. It repeats the application in adjectives and pushes evidence down the page.

hints.text: What does a reader need first to judge a student?
A student is judged by education and projects before jobs.
Contact, education, projects, experience, skills and interests. Drop the objective.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the strongest evidence for a student near the top.

byKey.obj: You kept the career objective. It uses space at the top for claims nobody can test.
byKey.left-out: You left out a section that belongs. Only the objective goes.

explain.text: Education comes first because it is what a student has most of. Projects come before experience when they show more of the skills the role tests. A career objective adds adjectives, not evidence.

screens.prose: Sam wants to keep "C++, Java, MATLAB". "Screens search for keywords," Sam says. "I did a C++ tutorial once."

rows: Proficient in Python, C++, Java, R, MATLAB, SQL

screens.question: Sam reaches a developer round. What happens?

options.text: The interviewer asks one C++ question; Sam cannot answer, and every other line now looks doubtful
Nothing; interviewers never read the skills line
options.why: You assumed the skills line is decoration. Interviewers often pick a language from it and start there.

options.text: The keywords pass the screen, and that is all that matters
options.why: You stopped at the screen. The line must also survive the interview that follows.

options.text: The long list shows ambition, which counts in Sam's favour
options.why: You read the list as ambition. An interviewer reads it as a claim and tests it.

hints.text: Which line would an interviewer use to start a developer round?
A listed language is an invitation to a question in it.
One C++ question ends the claim, and the interviewer starts doubting the rest.

feedback.correct: A padded line costs more than it gains.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the line into the interview.

byKey.ignored: You assumed nobody reads the skills line. In a coding round it is often the first thing asked about.
byKey.screen: You optimised for the screen alone. Padding that passes the screen fails in the room.
byKey.ambition: You thought more languages show ambition. They show claims, and each one can be tested.

explain.text: A listed language is a promise that you can be tested in it. One failed question undoes the line and casts doubt on the others. Put a language on only when you could pass a round in it.

screens.prose: An edge case. Jo studies physics and has never worked in finance. Jo's only job is a part-time supermarket shift lead.

rows: Shift lead, a supermarket, 2 years part-time

screens.question: How should Jo write the job?

options.text: Put projects first, then write the job for its skill: "Planned rotas for 14 staff; cut overtime by 12% in 3 months"
Leave the job off, since it is not finance
options.why: You hid real evidence. Leading people and working with numbers are skills an interviewer can test.

options.text: Write "Retail experience" with no detail
options.why: You kept it vague. A job with no result is another line with nothing to test.

options.text: Call it "inventory trading"
options.why: You stretched the truth. One follow-up question would expose it, and the CV would lose trust.

hints.text: What does the job show that a trading firm cares about?
Rotas are planning; overtime is a number.
Projects go first; the job stays, written for the skill it shows, with a result.

feedback.correct: Projects first, and the job written for its skill.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the job and show what skill it proves.

explain.text: Many applicants have no finance experience, and trading firms state none is needed (l1, as reported October 2026). Lead with projects, then write any job for the skill it shows, with a number. "Planned rotas for 14 staff; cut overtime by 12%" is testable and true.

screens.prose: Every line you kept followed one pattern: $$\text{line} = \text{verb} + \text{what you did} + \text{tool} + \text{a number you can defend}$$ A line with any part missing gives the interviewer less to test.

rows: Cut a weekly report from 3 hours to 20 minutes with a Python script

screens.question: Which line has all four parts?

options.text: Built a Python model of a card game's odds; matched the exact answer to 3 decimal places
Python, card games, probability
options.why: You picked a list. It has tools and topics but no verb and no result.

options.text: Built a model of a card game in Python
options.why: You picked a line with no number. The interviewer cannot tell how well it worked.

options.text: Worked out a card game's odds to 3 decimal places
options.why: You picked a line with no tool. Say whether it was code, a spreadsheet or by hand.

hints.text: Check each line for a verb, a task, a tool and a number.
Three of the lines each miss one part.
"Built a Python model ... matched the exact answer to 3 decimal places" has all four.

feedback.correct: Verb, task, tool and a number.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the line with all four parts.

explain.text: "Built" is the verb, the card game's odds the task, Python the tool, and 3 decimal places the number. Remove any part and the line is harder to test. Sam's report line follows the same pattern.

screens.prose: **Follow-up.** Interviewers push on a line. Sam's new line says a backtest's run time fell from 40 to 6 minutes. "How?" the interviewer asks. Pace: decide in under a minute, as you would aloud.

rows: Cleaned 2 years of daily prices for 500 shares in pandas; cut a backtest from 40 to 6 minutes

screens.question: Which answer defends the line?

options.text: "The loop recomputed returns for every share each day. I computed them once, in one pandas step, and reused them."
"I optimised the code until it was faster."
options.why: You restated the claim. The interviewer asked how, and this gives no method.

options.text: "A colleague did the speed-up; I ran the tests."
options.why: Honest, but then the line is not Sam's. Rewrite the line before sending the CV.

options.text: "It is hard to explain in the time we have."
options.why: You declined the question. Every line on the CV should take under a minute to explain.

hints.text: A defence names what was slow and what changed.
Before: the same work done again each day. After: done once.
Name the waste (recomputing returns) and the fix (computing once, then reusing).

feedback.correct: A cause, a fix and the tool.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the answer that explains the speed-up.

byKey.other: You picked the honest answer that sinks the line. Fix the line before it reaches an interviewer.

explain.text: The answer names what was slow, what changed and the tool used. The next push might be "how much faster?": $40 / 6 \approx 6.7$ times. Prepare one answer like this for every line you write.

screens.prose: Your turn, in your head first. Write your strongest project as one line in the pattern. Then judge three lines against the rubric: a verb, a number, a tool, a testable result.

rows: Built a Python backtest of 12-month momentum on 20 years of UK shares; net Sharpe 0.4 after a 10 bp cost
Passionate about quantitative finance and machine learning
Wrote a C++ order-book simulator; matched 1 million orders in 0.8 s, checked against a Python version

screens.question: Select all that apply: which lines meet every rubric point?

options.text: Line A
Line C
Line B
options.why: You kept an adjective line. "Passionate" has no verb, number or result to test.

hints.text: Check each line for a verb, a number, a tool and a result.
One line has no verb and no number.
A and C each have all four. B has none of them.

feedback.correct: A and C. You write your own CV in homework 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only lines with a verb, a number, a tool and a result.

explain.text: Lines A and C each name a verb, a tool, a number and a result that can be checked. Line B is a feeling, not a claim. You write your own CV, one page, in homework 2.

ideas: Every line on a CV is a claim an interviewer can test, and some will.
A strong line is a verb, what you did, a tool and a number you can defend.
UK student CV: one page, no photo, no date of birth, a predicted or achieved grade, projects before jobs.

formula.name: A CV line
formula.note: "Cut a weekly report from 3 hours to 20 minutes with Python."

summary.trap: Padding the skills line with languages from one tutorial: one question in each ends the claim.

quiz.question: Which line is the weakest on a CV?

options.text: Responsible for client reporting
Cut month-end reporting from 2 days to 4 hours with SQL
options.why: That line has a verb, a tool and a number. It is strong.

options.text: Predicted First; year 2 average 71%
options.why: A predicted grade is a checkable fact.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line with nothing to test.

explain.text: "Responsible for" names a duty, not something you did. The other two give a result or a checkable fact.

quiz.question: Select all that apply: which belong on a UK undergraduate CV?

options.text: A predicted or achieved grade
Dates for each degree and job
A photo
options.why: You added a photo. UK CVs leave it off.

options.text: A date of birth
options.why: You added a date of birth. It says nothing about skill and is left off.

feedback.correct: Grade and dates, no photo or date of birth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep facts about your work; drop personal details.

explain.text: A UK student CV gives a grade and dates, on one page. A photo and a date of birth are left off.

quiz.question: You once followed a short Rust tutorial. Your CV goes to a developer role next week.

options.text: Leave Rust off until you have used it for real work
List it; nobody checks every language
options.why: You assumed nobody checks. Developer rounds often start from the skills line.

options.text: List it as "Rust (advanced)"
options.why: You overstated a tutorial. One question would show the level.

feedback.correct: Off until you can be tested in it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what happens if the interviewer picks that language.

explain.text: A listed language invites a question in it. One tutorial will not survive that question, so the line costs trust. Add it once you have built something with it.

quiz.question: A second-year with two good projects and one weekend café job. What comes straight after education?

options.text: Projects
The café job
options.why: You put the job first. For a student, projects usually show more of what the role tests.

options.text: A career objective
options.why: You added an objective. It is adjectives, not evidence.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Lead with your strongest evidence.

explain.text: A student is judged on education and projects first. The café job still goes in, written for the skill it shows.
